prose_changes.old: In 1098 a group of monks walked out of the great Burgundian abbey of Molesme because they thought Benedictine life had grown too comfortable — Cluny and the other rich houses above all. And settled in a marshy clearing called Cîteaux to keep the Rule of St Benedict as plainly as they could: bare churches, simple food, no elaborate liturgy, and their own hands in the fields. Within a generation the reform had a constitution, the Carta Caritatis, binding every daughter house to the mother house through annual visitation and a yearly general chapter, and after Bernard of Clairvaux arrived in 1113 the order spread across Europe at extraordinary speed. Much of the actual labor was done by lay brothers, the conversi, who took vows but lived a separate, largely manual life alongside the choir monks on farms called granges. The order never ended, and its writers — Bernard on the Song of Songs, Aelred of Rievaulx on friendship — stayed among the most-read spiritual authors of the Latin West for centuries afterward.

prose_changes.old: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began living out a simple, demanding vision of penitence — plain dress, manual labor, and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society. And called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 they were condemned alongside the Waldensians for preaching without official permission, but where the Waldensians' story became one of lasting separation, theirs took the opposite turn. Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three recognized orders. Two religious, one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For roughly two centuries afterward they remained a real presence in northern Italian towns, their rule and community records still surviving, until the movement was formally suppressed by papal bull in 1571.

They refused the oaths and the violence that feudal society expected. They called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 Pope Lucius III condemned the Waldensians for preaching without leave. Later writers say he condemned the Humiliati with them. If so, their story then took the opposite turn. The Waldensians stayed apart for good, but Pope Innocent III took the Humiliati back in 1201. He made them three recognized orders. Two were religious orders. The third was for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For about two centuries they were a real presence in the towns of northern Italy. Their rule and community records still survive. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the order of Humiliati brothers.
